title: Direction Sense Basics
tagline: Year 1 Foundation — Turns, distances and final positions on a compass

introduction.overview: Direction sense questions describe a person walking and turning, and ask for the final direction, the distance from the starting point, or the direction of one place from another. The four main directions are North, East, South and West, and the four in-between directions are North-east, South-east, South-west and North-west. The best method is to draw the path on paper with North at the top, and to use the Pythagoras theorem when the final distance is diagonal.
introduction.placementRelevance: Direction questions are commonly asked in company reasoning rounds. They are short, need no theory beyond a compass and the right-angled triangle, and reward neat sketches.
introduction.realWorldContext: Reading a map, giving directions to a delivery partner, planning a drone path and following a compass in an outdoor survey all depend on the same ideas.

learningObjectives: Know the eight compass directions and which are opposite
Track the facing direction after left and right turns
Compute the net displacement from several legs of a path
Use the Pythagoras theorem for diagonal distances
Use sun and shadow facts for morning and evening questions

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Pythagoras theorem: in a right-angled triangle, hypotenuse² = base² + height². Common triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25.

coreDefinitions: Cardinal directions: North, East, South, West. Each is at 90° from the next one going clockwise.
Intermediate directions: North-east, South-east, South-west, North-west, lying halfway between the cardinals.
Opposite directions: North–South, East–West, North-east–South-west, North-west–South-east.
Right turn = 90° clockwise. Left turn = 90° anticlockwise. A U-turn is 180°.
Displacement: the straight-line distance and direction from the starting point to the final point (not the total length walked).
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Treat the ground as a graph with North as up (+y) and East as right (+x). Every leg of the walk changes x or y. At the end, subtract the opposite moves (North against South, East against West) and what remains is the displacement. The final distance is then a simple horizontal, vertical or diagonal measurement.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Imagine you are standing on the origin of a graph. Facing North, a right turn makes you face East, then South, then West, then North again. Left turns go the other way round: North → West → South → East.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Turning rule (clockwise order)
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: North → East → South → West → North for right turns
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Left turns follow the opposite order.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Net displacement
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Net x = East − West;  Net y = North − South
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: 4 km S then 4 km N cancels in y

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Straight-line distance
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Pythagoras on the net x and net y.
importantRulesAndFormulas.whenToUse: When the end point is diagonal from the start.
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: 3 km north then 4 km east → 5 km

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Sun and shadow
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Morning: sun in the East, shadow falls West. Evening: sun in the West, shadow falls East.
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: A shadow falls opposite to the sun.
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Facing the rising sun, the shadow falls behind the person

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Direction between two points
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Compare the net x and net y of the second point with the first
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Right and up = North-east, and so on.
importantRulesAndFormulas.whenToUse: Questions asking "in which direction is C from A".
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: C is 5 east and 5 south of A → South-east

mainNarrative: Start every question by drawing a small compass with North at the top. Mark the starting point and draw each leg with an arrow, labelling distances. After each turn, write the facing direction beside the arrow so that you never confuse left and right.

Facing direction after a turn is a rotation. Starting from North: right → East, right → South, right → West. A left turn from West leads to South. For two turns (such as right then right) the person faces the opposite direction, which is a U-turn.

Compute the net displacement by adding the legs along each axis. For a walk of 8 km North, 6 km East, 8 km South and 3 km West, the North and South legs cancel (8 − 8 = 0) and the East and West legs leave 6 − 3 = 3 km East. So the person is 3 km East of the starting point.

When the end point is diagonal, use the Pythagoras theorem. A man who walks 13 km East, 12 km North and 8 km West ends up 13 − 8 = 5 km East and 12 km North of the start, so the distance is √(5² + 12²) = 13 km.
For shadow problems, remember that a shadow falls opposite to the sun. At sunrise the sun is in the East, so shadows point West. At sunset the sun is in the West, so shadows point East.

deepDiveAspects.title: Diagonal directions
deepDiveAspects.content: North-east means equal parts North and East, i.e. 45° between them. If A is 5 km north of B and C is 5 km east of B, then from A to C you go 5 km east and 5 km south: C is South-east of A.

deepDiveAspects.title: Distance walked versus displacement
deepDiveAspects.content: A man who walks 4 km South and then 4 km North has walked 8 km but his displacement is zero. Be clear about which one the question asks for.

problemVariations.description: Left and right turns from a given direction.
problemVariations.exampleSnippet: Facing North, turn right then right again.

problemVariations.description: Compass direction of the final point.
problemVariations.exampleSnippet: 4 km South, 3 km West, 4 km North.
Facing the sun in the morning.

problemVariations.description: Relative positions of A and C.
problemVariations.exampleSnippet: C is east and south of A.

solvedExamples.title: Straight-line distance
solvedExamples.question: A man walks 3 km North, then turns right and walks 4 km. How far is he from the starting point, and in which direction?
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Draw the legs and use the Pythagoras theorem.

steps.title: Draw the first leg
steps.explanation: Facing North, he walks 3 km up.

steps.title: Turn right
steps.explanation: From North, a right turn faces East. He walks 4 km East.

steps.title: Find the direction
steps.explanation: The end point is 3 km North and 4 km East of the start, so it is North-east.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The two legs are at right angles, forming a 3-4-5 triangle.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Adding the legs (7 km) instead of using the straight-line distance.

solvedExamples.title: Cancelling opposite moves
solvedExamples.question: A man walks 4 km South, then 3 km West, and then 4 km North. How far is he from the starting point and in which direction?
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Net north-south movement and net east-west movement.

steps.title: North-south movement
steps.explanation: 4 km South and 4 km North cancel out: net 0.

steps.title: Combine
steps.explanation: He is 3 km from the start, to its West.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The two vertical legs have equal length in opposite directions.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Adding all three distances to get 11 km.

solvedExamples.title: Diagonal path with a return leg
solvedExamples.question: A man walks 13 km East, then 12 km North and then 8 km West. How far is he from the starting point?
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Net x and net y, then Pythagoras.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Using 13 and 12 directly without subtracting the westward leg.

shortcutMethods.title: Coordinate bookkeeping

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Draw and measure every leg step by step.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Keep two running totals, x (East positive) and y (North positive). Update them as you read the legs. The final answer is a distance √(x² + y²) and a compass direction from the signs of x and y.

rulesForApplication: Right turn = clockwise; left turn = anticlockwise.
Two turns of the same kind give a U-turn.
A shadow falls opposite to the sun.
Use the 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17 triples to see distances immediately.

commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Write the facing direction after every turn.

commonMistakes.mistake: Adding distances instead of finding displacement
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Cancel opposite moves and use Pythagoras for the diagonal.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Assuming the shadow falls towards the sun.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: The shadow is always on the opposite side from the sun.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mixing up the person's direction and the position
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Facing East but located to the West of the start.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Facing direction and position are different; track both.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Quickly eliminate options in the wrong quadrant after finding the signs of net x and net y.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Always draw. The drawing takes 15 seconds and prevents most errors.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Direction sense is a skill where neat sketches matter more than speed in calculation.

summaryBullets: Cancel opposite moves, then use Pythagoras.
Shadow falls opposite to the sun.

keyTakeaways: Draw the path with North at the top.
Keep running totals of x and y.
Check the question: direction faced or position?
selfCheckQuestions: Can I give the direction faced after turning right and then left from North?
Can I compute the straight-line distance after 6 km East and 8 km North?
Can I give the direction of the shadow in the evening?
